subject: mechanical
audience: FE Mechanical candidates and mechanical engineering students
title: The Sealed Tank That Reached 150 kPa, Not 133
featured_title: THE SEALED TANK THAT REACHED 150 KPA, NOT 133

presentation.challenge: The gas temperature rose from 300 K to 450 K. The pressure did not scale with Celsius temperature.

practice.primary_question: Why must absolute temperature be used when relating pressure and temperature of an ideal gas at constant volume?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Using Celsius temperatures directly in P1/T1=P2/T2 instead of absolute Kelvin or Rankine.

case_dna.target_misconception: For a sealed rigid tank, pressure can be scaled using the ratio of temperatures expressed in degrees Celsius.
case_dna.why_plausible: The temperature change is often stated in Celsius, so it is tempting to use those numbers directly in a ratio.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: At constant mass and volume for an ideal gas, P/T is constant only when T is absolute. Raising T from 300 K to 450 K raises 100 kPa to 150 kPa.
case_dna.corrected_model: For a fixed mass of ideal gas in a rigid tank, P1/T1=P2/T2 with T in Kelvin or Rankine.

problem_statement: A sealed rigid tank contains an ideal gas initially at 100 kPa and 300 K. The tank is heated until the gas reaches 450 K. A calculation using Celsius temperatures predicts the wrong final pressure. Determine the correct final pressure and identify why absolute temperature is required.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The tank was rigid. The pressure still rose by 50%.
gates.prompt: Which temperature scale belongs in the ideal-gas pressure ratio?

options.label: Use P1/T1=P2/T2 with T in Kelvin
options.reason: Ideal-gas relations involving temperature ratios require absolute temperature.

options.label: Use the same ratio with temperatures in Celsius
options.reason: Celsius zero is not thermodynamic zero, so direct temperature ratios are invalid.

options.label: Pressure stays constant because the tank is sealed
options.reason: A sealed rigid tank fixes mass and volume, not pressure.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the final pressure
gates.prompt: What final pressure (kPa) results when temperature rises from 300 K to 450 K?

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the pressure-temperature relation
gates.hint: Use the Kelvin temperatures exactly as given.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The ideal-gas law reduces cleanly at fixed mass and volume

cards.text: For fixed m and V, P/T is constant.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the tank calculation
report: C1. The gas mass is fixed.
C2. The tank volume is fixed.
C3. Temperature ratios may be formed directly with Celsius values.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Thermodynamic temperature ratios must use an absolute scale.

evidence_choices.label: Using 300 K and 450 K gives P2=150 kPa
evidence_choices.reason: This follows directly from the ideal-gas law.

correction.template: Using absolute temperature, the final pressure is {p2} kPa.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Limit the final pressure to 130 kPa
gates.constraint: Keep the same rigid tank and initial state.

options.label: Keep 450 K and expect pressure to remain 130 kPa
options.reason: At fixed volume, 450 K produces 150 kPa.

options.label: Subtract 273 from both temperatures before taking the ratio
options.reason: That converts to Celsius and breaks the absolute-temperature relation.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the rigid-tank relation
gates.prompt: A rigid ideal-gas tank is at 200 kPa and 400 K. If heated to 500 K, what pressure results?

options.label: 300 kPa
options.reason: That does not follow the constant-volume ratio.

options.label: 200 kPa
options.reason: Pressure changes with temperature at constant volume.

gates.explanation: For fixed ideal-gas mass and volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the ideal-gas state change
gates.confirmation: I confirm that temperature ratios in ideal-gas relations must use an absolute temperature scale.

items.label: What failed
items.value: A temperature ratio was formed using a nonabsolute scale.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Thermodynamic zero matters in gas-law ratios.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use P/T=constant at fixed mass and volume, with T in Kelvin or Rankine.

seo.seo_title: Ideal Gas Constant Volume: Why 100 kPa Becomes 150 kPa | FE E-051
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Mechanical Case E-051: a rigid ideal-gas tank heated from 300 K to 450 K rises from 100 kPa to 150 kPa.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Mechanical ideal gas constant volume
seo.excerpt: A rigid tank does not keep pressure constant. For an ideal gas, pressure tracks absolute temperature when mass and volume are fixed.
seo.direct_answer: For a fixed mass of ideal gas in a rigid tank, P/T is constant when temperature is absolute. Starting at 100 kPa and 300 K, heating to 450 K gives P2=100(450/300)=150 kPa.

faqs.q: Why must Kelvin be used in ideal-gas temperature ratios?
faqs.a: Because gas-law proportionalities require absolute thermodynamic temperature.

faqs.q: What happens to ideal-gas pressure in a rigid tank when absolute temperature rises 50%?
faqs.a: Pressure also rises 50%, assuming fixed mass and ideal-gas behavior.
